# H. WITS <note>Herman Witsius (1636–1708) was a leading Dutch theologian of the Further Reformation, known for reconciling different theological schools of thought.</note>
## PREFACE,
->*To the Opening of this Work, along with some useful*<-
->*Remarks concerning the same.*<-

---

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut containing an ornamental initial letter 'S' surrounded by dense, curling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>So rich is the All-sufficiency <term>Algenoegsaamheyt</term> <note>A central Protestant doctrine (Sola Scriptura) suggesting the Bible contains everything necessary for a person’s spiritual needs and salvation.</note> of the Holy *Scripture*, that whoever reads it with a humble, teachable, and attentive heart, being themselves illuminated with the light of the Spirit, finds therein in abundance all that they must know, believe, and do, in order to become eternally blessed. All its *doctrines* are so pure, and presented in such meaningful expressions; all its *commandments* so godly and virtuous, and urged with such powerful motives; its *examples* so remarkable, and of such elevated piety; especially that of the Lord JE-*SUS*, who is Living Virtue and Holiness: that nothing more precise, more beautiful, or more attractive can be imagined. For this reason, nothing sweeter, more useful, more edifying, or more enchanting can be found for a devout soul than to delight in leafing through this Divine Book and meditating upon the truths contained therein. Here the soul sees the faith of the Patri- <note>The text breaks off at "Aarts-", the beginning of "Aartsvaders" (Patriarchs).</note>

<summary>Herman Witsius begins his preface by extolling the beauty and "all-sufficiency" of the Bible, arguing that it contains everything a person needs for eternal salvation and moral guidance.</summary>
<keywords>Herman Witsius, Holy Scripture, sufficiency of scripture, piety, Jesus Christ, salvation, Dutch theology, Reformers</keywords>

--- Page 25 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface by Herman Witsius. The previous page ended mid-word with "Patri-", which is completed here as "Patriarchs" (Aartsvaders). This section contrasts the purity and zeal of the early Church with the perceived corruption and "outwardness" of later religious traditions.</meta>

# PREFACE.

-archs, Fathers, Prophets, and Apostles, in their simplest form; their zeal and godliness <term>Godvruchtigheyt</term> <note>A central concept in the Dutch "Nadere Reformatie" (Further Reformation), referring to a deeply personal, active, and heart-felt piety rather than mere ritual.</note> at its most fervent; their heavenly-mindedness most wonderful; and all their other virtues, adorned with a sincerity, modesty, and kindness without equal. And it must be a hardened, stony, indeed steeled mind that is not pricked, convinced, and more or less moved to imitation by all these things. 

Furthermore, one will nowhere else find these same matters in such full power and shining luster. For not gradually, but very quickly, the simplicity of early Christianity began to be marred, and spirituality began to be corrupted <note>original: "verbaſtert", meaning bastardized or degenerated from a pure state</note> by outward and self-invented displays. Yet the closer to the times of the Apostles, and of those who had seen and heard **JESUS** in the flesh, the purer it was: fewer ceremonies, more godliness; less outwardness, more inwardness; less conceit <note>original: "waanwijsheyt", literally "delusional wisdom" or intellectual arrogance</note>, and a greater, more active faith. 

When the soul was still ignited by the examples of the first Apostles of the Cross <term>Kruysgefanten</term> <note>Literally "Cross-envoys"; a term used for the early martyrs and missionaries who spread the Gospel under the banner of the cross.</note>, and the ears still glowed from their heavenly lessons of virtue, and the fire of the Pentecost feast <note>original: "Pinxterfeeſtes"</note> still burning spread its flames far and wide; then truly Christianity was a very different matter than it has become over the course of time. Since then, the itchiness— <note>The text breaks off at "jeuckerighey-", likely a reference to the "itching ears" mentioned in 2 Timothy 4:3, describing a desire for novel or self-serving doctrines.</note>

<meta>catchword: der</meta>

<summary>Witsius describes the superior piety and simplicity of the early Church, arguing that the closer one is to the time of Jesus and the Apostles, the purer the faith remains before being corrupted by human invention.</summary>
<keywords>Early Church, Piety, Apostles, Simplicity, Godliness, Pentecost, Corruption of Faith, Herman Witsius</keywords>

--- Page 26 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface by Herman Witsius. The previous page ended with the catchword "gel-", which likely began a word like "gelijck" (likewise) or "gelukkigh" (happily), leading into the description of how the early fervor was lost when the "lust for disputing" entered the church.</meta>

->H. WITS<-

the lust for disputing entered therein, and has disastrously torn apart the hearts that were previously so amiably united in love. Since then, people have adopted that which was glittering in Judaism <term>Jodendom</term> and Paganism <term>Heydendom</term>; with which Christianity has not been so much adorned as it has been bloated and stifled. Since then, the world with its riches, luxury, and pomp has broken in; and when the church buildings were decorated with marble and silver and gold, the Christian Church lost her most precious **soul-ornament** <note>original: "zielcieraad," referring to inner spiritual beauty and purity of character.</note>. 

And therefore, when one steps outside the Holy Scriptures, Christianity is never to be seen in a more beautiful form than in its first centuries, when it struggled with its poverty and contempt. Being splattered with the blood of the **Martyrs**, the scrapings and dregs of all <note>original: "aller affschrapsel en uytvaagsel." This is a biblical allusion to 1 Corinthians 4:13, where Apostles are described as the "scum of the earth" or the "refuse of the world."</note>, it was a spectacle for Angels and for men. 

Therefore, those who bring to light the customs of the Christians of those centuries from the histories of Christian Antiquity <term>Aaloudheyt</term> and from the writings of the first Fathers, and display them for the conviction of these later times, perform a laudable service to the common cause of virtue. To this end serves this present book, titled ***PRIMITIVE CHRISTIANITY*** <note>original: "HET EERSTE CHRISTENDOM." This is a Dutch translation of William Cave's "Primitive Christianity," first published in English in 1672.</note>, written with precise learning, neatness of judgment, and a pleasing style, in the En-

The truth undoubtedly lies between both positions: It is clear from Church Histories and many passages in *Tertullian*, *Cyprian*, and others, that in the very first centuries of Christianity, for the establishment of the doctrine and discipline of the Church, many *Synods* and *Councils* were held, although their decrees are not available today under those names of *Synods* and *Councils*. Now, a portion of those decrees—namely, those concerning Church customs and discipline—we can understand to have been collected by certain men of learning and judgment, likely around the beginning of the third century. He who opposes *Him* mocks all the foolish stirrings
Of *Jew* and *Heathen*, throws their priestly throne to the earth,
And makes his *Christian Church* raise its head in victory.
The Lord pours, on the day of the high *Pentecost feast*,
From Heaven’s Upper Hall, the Spirit upon his emissaries;
So visibly, that all the people, having flowed from all sides
To the house at the great sound, are amazed and afraid.
There they hear *God’s* great deeds reported together,
Each in his own language; one sees how the holy fire—
Not that which consumed so many a *Lamb*, or *Ram*, or *sacrificial Bull*,
But the *Antitype* <note>original: "Teegenbeeld" — a theological term meaning the reality that fulfills an Old Testament symbol or "type."</note>, *God’s Spirit*, sits upon these heroes.
This fire, whose great power is never kept confined,
Comes breaking out violently, as if in bright flames,
Flies through *Palestine*, to the most unknown regions
Where *Greek* or *Roman* power had built its seat.
No idol is able to ward off *Christ’s* teaching;
The oracles, so famous, all fall silent together;
The devils, through the power of the World-Savior’s name,
See themselves forced to return to the pool of the abyss.
Stubborn *Israel*, conceited of its lineage
As *Abraham’s* true seed, though degenerated from that father
Through the vile murder of the Prince and Vein of Life,
Sees at once both temple service and state brought to nothing.
Thus the *Church* triumphs! Firmly riveted in the blood of the Cross
Of God’s Son; established by his Spirit and power:
Thus the darkness retreats before the all-radiating Light!
Thus the *World* sees itself gifted with the highest salvation!
The *Church*, thus firmly built, grows with the years,
(Though the *World’s* supreme power, with wide-gaping jaws,
Goes vomiting out its malice to suppress her seed)
And remains unshakable upon her firm Cornerstone:
She suffers, with tough patience, the *Ten Persecutions* <note>original: "Tien Vervollegingen" — referring to the traditional historical periods of Roman persecution against Christians, ending with the Edict of Milan.</note>,
With which the *Roman* Empire fiercely beset her,
So that street and market constantly smoke with the blood of the Saints;
Yet she comes leaping out of shackles and bonds under *Constantine*.
This greatest Emperor’s care extends mostly to *Jesus's Church*,
Enriches her with a brilliance and royal treasures,
Lends crown and imperial scepter to make his realm encompass her,
So that his whole goal and aim is for God’s temple-work.

The peace obtained for CHRIST’S Church through his Predecessor's <note>A reference to Constantine the Great, who first legalized Christianity, or his sons who followed him.</note> favor.
He attempts, with the devil’s cunning, to reintroduce

He goes lurking like a cruel Bear by CHRIST’S sheepfold;
Yet, struck by an arrow, he dies most unexpectedly.
His death makes Heathendom give its last death-rattle,
And Christianity enjoys full freedom-rest once more;
One sees the war-torch extinguished and quenched,
And CHRIST’S peaceful people living in peace anew.
How shall they live? According to the Law of Heathen or of Jew?
Far from it: Prince JESUS’ mouth teaches us far higher matters,
Showing that man can never reach the Kingdom of Heaven,
Unless the "Old Man" <note>A theological term referring to the sinful nature of humanity which must be "put off," according to the teachings of St. Paul.</note> is killed through His death on the Cross.
He points to a narrow Gate to receive the Crown of Life,
A small and steep path sown with sharp thorns:
He shows how the fruit of Righteousness is harvested in peace,
For those who ascend to Heaven along the path of virtue.
The first Christian people prove, by their conduct,
How deeply their Master's teaching penetrated their hearts;
They never leave Heaven’s path, no matter how hard assailed by the Cross,
So that the image of CHRIST may be displayed in them.
This is shown to us by CAVE <note>William Cave (1637–1713), a prominent English church historian whose works were widely translated.</note>, who, well-versed in the pages of Antiquity,
Describes Ancient Christianity with a learned Quill,
Who most clearly displays to the Christian people,
From the Ancient Fathers, the first state of the Church and all its deeds.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'W' with scrolling floral patterns and a sunburst motif.</image-desc>
What many excellent books does our century not produce
For benefit and edification? From every corner
The world is instructed: thus one finds in Cave’s
Work, the state of the ancient and First Church <note>original: "Eerste Kerk" — referring to the "Primitive" or Apostolic church of the first three centuries.</note>
Of the Christians very neatly contained. One sees here how they lived in former times,
And how the Heathens <note>original: "Heydenen" — refers to the non-Christian subjects and authorities of the Roman Empire.</note> opposed their religion;
How Christ’s true doctrine, through cunning and violence,
Was falsely accused, plagued, persecuted, and tormented.
And how the Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers," the influential early theologians and bishops of the first few centuries.</note> strongly opposed this
With their reasoning and practice, and desired that one should not pass
Judgment against them through blind passion,
But in sincerity and according to the Holy Scripture.
He makes a sketch of the Church structure <note>original: "Kerkgebouw" — here used metaphorically to describe the "edifice" or organizational structure of the early Christian community rather than a physical building.</note> and who governed
The churches and their service, and how the worship was conducted,
At the time and place appointed for it, and entirely
How Holy Baptism was administered, and the Lord's Supper. <note>original: "Avondmaal" — the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>
Their life was, he shows, a series of all virtues,
With which they gladdened Heaven's host and the Sovereign Lord;
They were humble, despising the earth
And the world’s trivial goods, and looked Heavenward.
They never adorned themselves with vain attire,
Nor constantly paraded with it, like peacocks on their feathers.

Very simple was their food and daily drink,
Their chastity also shone forth in their conduct,
They were unshakable, so that no heavy distress,
Of pain or of promise, could hold them back
From their confession; no sorrowful slavery
Ensnared them, not even the cruelest tyranny;
Their word was "Yes" <note>A reference to the biblical injunction in Matthew 5:37: "Let your 'Yes' be 'Yes.'"</note>: Their affections
Moved them to spend their goods voluntarily
For the service of the Brotherhood: Peaceableness shone in them
And humble subjection under their authorities:
Also in use among them were Church discipline and judgment,
Which, conducted according to God's word, brought great benefit and advantage,
But all this could provide no delight to our nation,
Until it was translated into our tongue.
Thus the Teacher BOR <note>D. Salomon Bor, the translator and minister at Zeist mentioned on the title page.</note>, driven by zeal,
Besides other work already published by Him,
Brought this stately English work into the Dutch language <note>original: "Nederduyts" — in the 17th century, this term referred to the Dutch language as spoken in the Low Countries.</note>,
So that it might also be for our edification.
Whoever then is inclined to delight himself,
And thoroughly understand the affairs of the first Christians,
Let him give himself with diligence to the earnest study
Of this well-wrought work and this translated book.
Now my desire would demand to dwell a little longer here,
And to spread abroad my FATHER’s name and praise,
And to express the merit of him who watches over the Lord’s Church,
And now, moreover, translates this glorious work.
But I break this off and say: Live long, renowned Writer <note>Refers to the original author, William Cave.</note>,
Live long, you who have translated it through untiring zeal:
Live long, learned Man, who thus writes in English,
Live long, he who is so driven by the desire for translating.

# Accused of Godlessness. Book 1, Chapter 1.

[When the enemy] saw that he could not carry out [his plans] through open attacks and assaults / he sought to work them out by undermining the same; he attempted to fill the minds of men with false and unjust prejudices against **Christianity** / and to weigh it down with entire burdens of reproach / insults, and dishonor / knowing no readier way / to prevent the acceptance of the same / than by corrupting it / and wounding its reputation. To that end, all the arts of slander and malice were summoned and mustered / and the **Christians** were shamelessly accused of all such crimes / that could bring them and their **Religion** into shame and contempt.

That which was now charged against the Christians / concerned either their *Religion*, or the Christians' external state and circumstances, or it concerned their life, morals, and conduct, alongside certain things / touching the matter or manner of their service; all of which we shall present and remark upon in order / how the **Christians** of that time defended themselves against such accusations.

The **Christian Religion** was, upon its first revelation in the world, vehemently accused of godlessness and novelty <note>In the Roman world, "novelty" (newness) in religion was seen as a sign of being illegitimate or dangerous; true religion was expected to be ancient.</note>. Regarding the first / it was commonly decried as a great *Atheism* <note>original: "Atheistery". In this historical context, "atheism" did not mean a denial of all gods, but specifically the refusal to worship the established Roman state gods.</note> and godlessness, as an affront to the religion of the pagans / and an undermining of the essence and existence of their **Gods** themselves; this was the content of their accusation / just as we [shall see] the same—

## CHAPTER II.

### *Of the Novelty with which Christianity was accused.*

### C O N T E N T S.

Christianity decried as a later and new teaching <note>In the Roman world, "novelty" in religion was seen as a sign of instability or lack of divine favor; ancient traditions were considered more valid simply by virtue of their age.</note>. This was a common accusation, still used when Christianity had already been in the world for several hundred years. This gave a great prejudice against Christianity. People were disinclined to forsake the Religion of their Ancestors. What the Christians answered to this. The Christian Religion in essence and effect is the same as that of the ancient Jews, and in that respect is by far the oldest Religion in the world: This shown and urged by *Tertullian*, *Clement of Alexandria*, *Eusebius*, and others. Its later emergence and novelty provide no immediate prejudice for reasonable and impartial people. The folly and vanity of clinging to absurd and unreasonable customs simply because they are old, and refusing to exchange one's views for a better one. An objection: if Christ and the Christian Religion were such great benefits for the human race, why...

<summary>This page concludes the defense against charges of atheism and introduces the common Roman criticism that Christianity was a "novel" or new-fangled religion, which lacked the legitimacy of ancient traditions.</summary>

## Chapter III.

### Concerning that which was charged against the Christians in regard to their outward circumstances.

->SUMMARY.<-

The Christians viewed and despised by the Pagans as a company of stupid and unlearned people, lowly women, and children. This accusation presented, and answered at length by *Origen*. <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was one of the most prolific and influential early Christian theologians and scholars.</note> Christianity provided with the true and best knowledge; it excludes no one, whether learned or unlearned. Christians not afraid to share the knowledge of their mysteries with the curious and impartial. The power of Christianity against the subtlest sects and greatest learning. The Christians accused of their poverty and insignificance. This accusation was generally false. Christianity accepted by persons of all ranks, from the highest as well as the lowest. Various examples thereof. *Fl. Clemens* and *Fl. Domitilla* (close relatives of *Domitian*), another *Domitilla*, niece of *Domitian*, *Acil. Glabrio* the Consul, <note>The Dutch text uses "Burgermeester" (Burgomaster), but in a Roman context, this refers to the office of *Consul*.</note> *Apollonius* the Senator, <note>The Dutch "Raadsheer" refers to a member of the Roman Senate.</note> and others were Christians. That the Emperor *Philip* <note>Philip the Arab, who reigned from 244 to 249 AD; later traditions often claimed he was the first Christian emperor, though this was debated.</note> was not a Christian is proven: the origin of that claim and from whence it came. Even if Christianity had not been confessed by such persons, this would not have been a well-founded prejudice against it. Outward greatness and state are not necessary to Religion. The advantage of the Christians resulting from their insignificance and the world's contempt. Concerning the accusation of them as a useless people, and one of no service to the public. This was

...was denied. The opinion that it was not permitted for Christians to bear arms, or to hold public offices, <note>Early Christian pacifism and their frequent refusal to serve in the Roman administration or military was a major point of contention with the Imperial authorities.</note> applied specifically only to some, and in certain cases, and why? How much the world was indebted to the Christians for drawing people back from sin and godlessness. The Gospel was a great tool for this; its common influence even upon those who were not converted by it. The writings of the philosophers were generally better after the rise of Christianity, and why? <note>The author suggests that the moral clarity of the Gospel forced pagan philosophers to improve their own ethical systems to compete.</note> The excellent prayer of *Simplicius*. <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490 – c. 560 AD) was one of the last Neoplatonist philosophers; his "Commentary on the Enchiridion of Epictetus" ends with a famous prayer to the "Father and Guide of our reason."</note> Christians were very beneficial through their manifold good deeds and miracles, healing the sick, raising the dead, and driving out devils, etc. This miracle-working power remained in the Church for some centuries. Christians were furthermore slandered as being harmful to the world, and a cause of all common evils and difficulties. This was repeatedly thrown at them. The occasion upon which *Augustine* and *Orosius* wrote a defense against this. <note>Following the Sack of Rome in 410 AD, Pagans blamed Christians for the disaster, claiming the old gods were angry. Saint Augustine wrote *The City of God* and Paulus Orosius wrote *Seven Books of History Against the Pagans* to refute these claims.</note> This accusation was rightly brought back against the Pagans, and they were sent to seek the cause of the common difficulties within themselves. Some of these are related by *Tertullian*. <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage who famously argued that if the Nile didn't flood or the Earth quaked, the Pagans immediately cried, "Away with the Christians to the lion!"</note> The Christians were wrongly accused of this, as the world was already plagued with such evils before Christianity appeared. The general state of affairs was better and more prosperous after the rise of Christianity than before. Its prosperity increased or decreased according to whether Christianity was well or poorly received in the world.

"...[to dip our hands] in the blood of the innocent: our swords know how to strike a rebel or an enemy, but not how to harm those who are citizens and innocent; we know that we have taken up our arms not against, but for our friends and fellow-citizens: we have always fought for justice, godliness, and for the safety of the innocent <note>original: "onnoselen." While "onnozel" means "silly" in modern Dutch, in this 17th-century context it refers to the "innocent" or "harmless."</note>. This has been the aim in all the dangers we have undergone until now: we have strived to be faithful, but how shall we be able to keep our faith with you, if we are not first faithful to our God?" So far were the Christians of those times from refusing the service of their Sovereigns: Even those who, through their particular views, judged such things to be forbidden <note>This refers to early Christian pacifists who believed any military service was incompatible with the teachings of Jesus.</note>, reckoned that it was compensated for by them in another way; And therefore, when Celsus <note>Celsus was a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and the first major intellectual opponent of Christianity.</note> urged the Christians to accept public offices and to help the Emperors in their wars, Origen (g) <margin>[g] Against Celsus, book 8, p. 426, 427.</margin> answered: "we do so; but through Divine, not through human helps, praying for their persons, and for their prosperity and welfare; we fight more than all men for the Emperor, since we occupy ourselves in the exercises of godliness, and fight for him through prayers." But besides that, there were still many other reasons by which the Christians defended themselves against the accusation of their <term>lack of service|original: "ondienst," meaning a failure to fulfill expected duties to the state or society</term> to men, of which I shall presently present only these two:

### Accused of Uselessness. Book 1. Section 3. Chapter H. ###

Firstly, they truly sought to lead people away from sin and godlessness toward a good and virtuous life. By this means, they did not only care for humanity's highest and most weighty concern—the interest of their souls and eternal happiness in another life—but they also greatly promoted the peace and prosperity of the places where they lived. For wicked and godless people are the pest and plague of the human race; through their evil examples and advice, they inflame and infect others, and bring God’s vengeance upon their places of residence. In contrast, the godly bring down the favor and blessing of Heaven, and lead others through their counsel and example toward godliness and honor. By this, the foundations of government and the well-being of civic life <note>original: "burgerlijk leven." This refers to the orderly functioning of a city or state.</note> are established and strengthened. In this regard, no one excelled as much as the *Christians* of old. Churches. Book I. Part 6. B.

# CHAPTER VI.

## *Concerning the Churches and Places of Public Worship in the Early Times.*

->CONTENTS<-

Place is a circumstance necessary for every action. The piety of Christians in building places for the formal practice of religion. They had, even in the times of the Apostles, their own separate places for public assemblies. This is proven from the New Testament. It also appears in the following centuries from the testimonies of the Early Church Fathers and pagan writers. The common objection of the pagans—that the Christians had no temples—is presented and answered. The number of churches increased when Christianity was better received; their condition under *Diocletian* <note>Roman Emperor (r. 284–305) who led the last and most severe persecution of Christians.</note>; the same restored and improved by *Maximus* and *Constantine*. The shape of their churches was oblong; built facing the East. The *vestibulum* <note>The entrance area or porch.</note>, portal, or forecourt. The *narthex* <note>An enclosed porch or entrance area in early Christian churches, often where penitents and those not yet baptized would stand.</note>, and what was contained therein. The nave or the body of the church. The *ambo* <note>A raised platform or pulpit used for reading the Gospel and Epistles.</note>, pulpit, and reading place; the standing area of the faithful. The <term>hierateion</term> <note>original Greek: "ἱερατεῖον"; the sanctuary or innermost holy place where the altar stood.</note>, or innermost place. The altar, or the Table of the Lord. The Bishop’s throne and the seating of the Elders. What the *diaconicon* <note>A vestry or sacristy where sacred vessels and vestments were kept.</note> was; the place named <term>prothesis</term> <note>The place or table where the bread and wine were prepared for the Eucharist.</note>. Afterward, the Christians decorated their churches. Whether they had altars in them. Appropriate tables for the administration of divine services. These were generally called "altars" by the Church Fathers, and in what sense. They did not have such decorated altars as the pagans had.

Of the Churches

...in their Temples, and [which] the Papists <note>A historical term, often used by Protestant authors of this period, to refer to Roman Catholics.</note> now have in their churches. When they began to make the Altars fixed and out of stone. [The churches] made into *asyla* <note>original Latin: "asyla"; places of sanctuary where fugitives or those seeking mercy could find protection from the law.</note> and places of refuge, and endowed with many privileges by the Christian Emperors. No Images in their Churches for four hundred years after Christ; this proven from the Early Church Fathers. The Paintings in the Churches condemned by the Council of *Illiberis* <note>The Council of Elvira (c. 306 AD), an early church council in Spain known for its strict canons, including a famous prohibition against images in churches.</note>. An account of the tearing of a Painting of Christ by *Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a bishop known for his fierce opposition to images in worship.</note> in the Church of *Anablatha*; a powerful proof from this against Image-worship. The <term>Encainia</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐγκαίνια"; the festival of dedication or the formal consecration of a new building.</note>, or the consecration of their Churches. Our Fairs <note>The Dutch word "Kermissen" derives from "Kerkmis" (Church-Mass), originally an annual festival held to celebrate the anniversary of a local church's dedication.</note> in memory of the consecration of this or that Church. What income or revenue they had in the first centuries. Some Churches had fixed incomes even under the Pagan Emperors. These were greatly increased by the Piety of *Constantine* and the first Christian Princes. Their laws regarding this noted. Their reverence shown by their arrival and presence in the Churches, even by the Emperors.

The first Christians were no more zealous against the idolatrous worship of the Pagan Gods than they were religiously mindful of everything concerning the honor and service of the true God—regarding its external practice and circumstances; as will soon become apparent, if we but consider what care they took regarding the place, the time, the persons, the materials, and the manner of service which they offered to God. We shall subsequently examine what is most noteworthy about each of these matters and pertains to them.

### Of the First Christians. Book I, Chapter 6.

...as far as the historical records of those times provide us with knowledge thereof.

<margin>[a]</margin> Place is an inseparable circumstance of religious service; since every body—by a natural necessity regarding its existence—requires a certain place, whether for rest or for movement. And therefore the service of God—which is for a large part an external act, especially when performed through the gathering of several persons—requires not only a place, but a place that can conveniently hold within its space all those who join together for the same public exercise of their religion. This reasoning moves all nations, even by the light of nature <note>The "light of nature" refers to the idea that human reason and logic alone, independent of divine revelation, can lead people to recognize certain truths, such as the need for a dedicated space for worship.</note>, to establish public places in honor of their gods,
<margin>(b) <unclear>...</unclear> p. 38</margin> and suited to their gatherings, in order to perform their religious services and devotions within them. But my present inquiry reaches no further than to the early Christians, and specifically not whether they gathered to perform their common duties (which I take as a certainty that no one can doubt), but whether they had fixed and appropriately prepared places for conducting their public services in their assemblies. That they indeed had such places even in those early times, I believe will be beyond dispute, if we briefly review those first centuries of Christianity. # Concerning the Churches

Since there is not a good and sufficient testimony / which can prove / that images were either worshipped, or used in the Churches, for about four hundred years after Christ; and I doubt not / but this could be shown for an even longer period of time / if my work were not primarily limited to those first centuries of Christianity.

->Of the Lord's Day, the Fast- and Feast-<-

### CONTENTS.

Time is as necessary for the practice of Religion as place. Set times of public Worship observed by all nations. The Lord's Day <note>Sunday, the first day of the week.</note> primarily observed by the Christians. Called Sunday, and why? Specially hallowed in memory of Christ’s resurrection. Kneeling in prayer forbidden on this day, and why. Their public assemblies were always held on this day. They were compelled in times of persecution to meet before daybreak: For this reason, mocked by the Heathens as *latebrosa & lucifugax natio* <note>Latin: "a skulking and light-shunning nation"</note>, a hiding and light-avoiding people. The Lord's Day always held as a day of joy. Fasting on the same forbidden. The great care of Constantine <note>Constantine the Great (reigned 306–337), the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity.</note> and the first Christian Emperors for the honor and maintenance of that day. Their laws regarding it. Their constant and conscientious observance of public service on the Lord's Day. The abuse of these memorial days in later times.

Time is a circumstance that is as inseparable from religious exercises as place; for man, consisting of soul and body, cannot always be actively occupied in the service of God, as that is a privilege of the Angels and Souls who are freed from the bonds of mortality. As long as we are here, we must serve God according to the circumstances of our present state, and as a necessary consequence, have some special and determined time to do so: And therefore, so that people in a matter of such great importance should not be left in loose uncertainty, people of all ages and nations have been led by the precept of nature itself to establish certain and suitable times at which they might assemble and come together for the performance of public religious exercises. Which and how many the public feast days among...

### of the Early Christians. Book 1. Chapter 7.

...of the Jews and Heathens were established and maintained is not currently my task to record. Regarding the ancient Christians, they always had their special and convenient opportunities, <margin>(d)</margin> their formal and fixed times, to come together for the performance of the common duties of Religion; among which the Lord's day, having precedence over all others, we shall make a beginning with it; and in order not to trouble myself with all the disputes which have arisen concerning it in these latter times, I shall only record some proofs of the piety of the Christians in respect to this day, which I have noted in reading the writers of that time.

Next to the Lord’s day, the Sabbath or Saturday (for the word *Sabbatum* <note>Latin for Sabbath; historically used by the Church Fathers to refer specifically to Saturday.</note> was always used in the writings of the Fathers whenever they spoke of it in relation to Christians) was held in great esteem by them / and was honored, especially in the East, with all the public ceremonies of Religion. To understand this, we must know that as the Gospel gained the upper hand in that region among the Jews (they usually being the first converted to the Christian faith), they continued to maintain a great reverence for the institutions of Moses, and especially for the Sabbath, as having been instituted by God himself (as a memorial of his rest from the work of creation), confirmed by their great Master Moses / and celebrated by their ancestors as the stately day of their public worship; and therefore they could not endure that the same should be entirely abolished and set aside. For this reason, the prudence of those times thought it good (as in other matters of Jewish Church customs, so also in this) to yield somewhat to the inclination of that people, and to keep the Sabbath as a day for religious exercises:

To speak briefly of this, the situation was as follows: The churches of Asia Minor held their Easter <note>Dutch: *Paaſchen*, referring to the Paschal feast</note> on the same day on which the Jews held theirs, namely, on the fourteenth day of the first month (which always began with the new moon), mostly corresponding to our March. This they did on whatever day of the week that fourteenth day fell upon; and because of this—namely, because they held their Easter on the *fourteenth moon* <note>original Latin: *quarta decima Luna*</note>, on the fourteenth day after the *appearance* <note>original Greek: *φάσις* (phasis), referring to the first sighting of the new moon</note> of the moon—they were called *Quartodecimans* <term>Quartodecimans: from the Latin for 'fourteenth', these early Christians insisted on celebrating the Paschal feast on the 14th of the month of Nisan, the same day as the Jewish Passover, regardless of whether it was a Sunday</term>, which means "fourteen-dayers." 

The other Churches, and especially those of the West, did not follow this custom, but held Easter on the Lord's day <note>Sunday</note>, which followed the day of the Jewish Passover; partly to show greater honor to that day <note>The day of the Resurrection</note>, and partly to distinguish between Jews and Christians. Those of Asia defended their view with the practice of the Apostles: "Polycarp, the Bishop of Smyrna, who had lived and conversed with them, had kept it on that day, as also Saint John and all the other Apostles," says Irenaeus (who had known Polycarp himself and without doubt heard this from his own mouth) in a letter regarding this matter, <margin>(h) Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, Book 5, chapter 24, page 193.</margin> although he himself was of a different opinion. But the Bishops of Asia paid little heed to what was said or done in Rome and kept to their old way. And although they lost ground through the diligent practices of the opposing party, they always found ways to maintain their cause until the time of Constantine <margin>(n) Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book 3, Chapters 14, 17.</margin>, who, noticing that this difference, along with others, greatly disturbed the peace of the Churches, for these and other reasons convened the Great Council of Nicaea <note>The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) was the first ecumenical council of the Christian Church.</note>. This council then formally issued its verdict on this dispute: that "Easter [should be celebrated] on one and the same day throughout the whole world..."

Next to this **Easter Feast**, in those early times, that of **Pentecost** was noteworthy; a Feast of great esteem among the Jews, in memory of the Law delivered at that time on Mount Sinai / and the gathering and bringing home of their harvest; and of no less [esteem] among the Christians, because of the descent of the **Holy Spirit** upon the Apostles and other Christians in the visible form of divided fiery tongues, which occurred on that day / and because of the miracle-working powers / communicated to them thereby. # Of the Feast Days

[I] will not dispute whether the same was always held on that day on which we now keep it, namely, the twenty-fifth of December; it seems probable that in the East it was held for a long time in January, under the name and the general season of the **Epiphany** <note>original: "Epiphania", meaning "manifestation" or "appearance"</note>, until, receiving more light on this matter from the Western Churches, they moved it to that day;

<margin>
(h) Sermon 31, volume 5, page 417.
</margin>

<margin>
(i) Homily 23, *On the Baptism of Christ* <note>original Latin: "de bapt. Christi"</note>, volume 1, page 278.
</margin>
The Feast of **Epiphany**, properly so-called, was held on the sixth of January, and bore that name because of a threefold revelation or appearance which was commemorated on that day; which events, although not occurring in the same year, were nonetheless said to have happened on the same day of the year. The first was the appearance of the Star, which led the Wise Men to Christ. The second was the famous appearance at the baptism of Christ, where all the persons of the Holy **Trinity** <note>original: "Drie-eenigheyt"</note> revealed themselves to the external senses: the Father in the voice from Heaven, the Son in the river **Jordan**, and the Holy Spirit in the visible form of a dove. This was always held as a principal Feast, and was, as Chrysostom (i) re-

# Of the Feast Days
<meta>catchword: it</meta>

In those sorrowful and bloody times, when the Christian Religion triumphed over persecution and gained more influence in the world through nothing else than the bold and steadfast suffering of its professors <note>original: "belijders"; those who publicly confessed their faith under the threat of death</note>, who could be deterred from it by no threats or pains; the people held great reverence for those who had suffered so much for the sake of Christianity and had laid down their lives to confirm its truth. They looked upon the **Confessors** (those who profess the faith) and **Martyrs** (blood-witnesses <note>original: "bloed-getuygen"; a literal translation of the Greek word 'martys'</note>) as the great champions of their Religion, who had resisted even unto blood and had died to seal its foundations and to uphold its honor and truth. Therefore, they judged it to be highly reasonable to pay all possible honor to their memory—partly so that others might be encouraged to similar patience and courage, and partly so that their virtue might not lose its reward even in this world.

For this reason, they were accustomed to gather once a year at the graves of the Martyrs, there to solemnly recount their sufferings and triumphs, to praise their virtues, and to thank God for their godly examples, for their holy lives, blessed deaths, and for their palm branches and crowns <note>Traditional symbols of victory and eternal life in early Christian art</note>. These annual solemnities were called *memoriæ martyrum* <note>Latin: "memories of the martyrs"</note>, the remembrances of the Martyrs;

# Of the Feast Days

...condemned such ceremonies—which were established solely for the prayers and memory of the pious, and for our encouragement and imitation. He desires that they ought to remember the seriousness and severity of our otherwise gentle and humble **Savior**, who drove the buyers and sellers out of the **Temple** when they, through their trade, had made the house of prayer into a den of thieves. And it is true that those annual commemorations, although in their first institution reasonable and praiseworthy, were nevertheless misused afterwards through the folly and stupidity of men, in order to serve them in their great superstition and <term>idolatries</term> <note>The author uses "idolatry" here to describe the transition from honoring martyrs as heroes to worshipping them as divine mediators.</note>. It is so certain that the best and most profitable things can be turned to evil and corrupted. For from this have arisen the doctrine and practice of praying to and invoking the **Saints**, and requesting their intercession with God; the service to **relics**, their **pilgrimages**, and the visiting of churches; the making of offerings at the graves of such and such **Saints**, and similar superstitious customs, which in the following centuries overran such a large part of the **Christian Church**. These were things, however, which were entirely unknown in the simplicity of the purer and better times.

### of the Early Church. Book I. Chapter 8. ###

...of the people, or those who were specifically set apart and hallowed for the public service of Religion. Concerning the body of the people, we may observe that when Christianity first began to be permitted in the large cities, all the believers of such a place commonly came together and assembled there; and the Christians from neighboring places likewise resorted thither at the times of public service. But as Religion gradually increased, the public Assembly—especially in the larger cities—soon began to grow too large and numerous to be managed with order and fitness. Therefore, they were necessitated to divide that body into particular assemblies, which had their own Pastors and spiritual Leaders. While these were placed over them, they nevertheless always remained under the oversight and care of him who was the President or Bishop of that place. Consequently, after the Church was able to arrange and establish its order and discipline, the people began to be distinguished—either by their age and practice, or by the nature of the condition in which someone then was—into various ranks and <term>classes</term> <note>original: "classen"; hierarchical groupings within the congregation</note>, which then had their distinct places in the Church and were admitted by degrees to the different parts of the public worship.

**St. Basil**, (d) reasoning about Church customs / and the teachings of Christianity / divides them into two parts: the **proclamations**, and the **doctrines**. The **proclamations** <note>original: κηρύγματα (kerygmata); public preachings or announcements of the gospel</note> were those parts of the Religion / which were allowed to be **made public** <note>original: δημοσιεύεσθαι (demosieuesthai); to be published or shared openly</note>, preached before the people / and presented in a common manner: The **doctrines** <note>original: δόγματα (dogmata); formal decrees or inner teachings</note> were the highest and more hidden teachings and parts of the Christian faith: and these were **secret** <note>original: ἀπόῤῥητα (aporrhēta); things not to be spoken of or "unmentionable" to the uninitiated</note>, things that one must not present thoughtlessly or in general / but to which one had to pay heed with silence: Of this nature were (e) the doctrines of the **Holy Trinity**, the personal union <note>This refers to the "Hypostatic Union," the theological doctrine that Jesus Christ is both fully God and fully man</note>, and similar things / especially of the two **Sacraments**, Baptism and the Lord's Supper: for although they made known to their young listeners as much of these as was necessary to awaken their desires for them, nevertheless, the primary essence of them / regarding the **sacramental signs**, the manner of their administration / and how God is present in the **Holy Supper** / the true purpose of all the secret ceremonies used therein, was kept hidden with all possible caution from outsiders,

<header>Of the Persons</header>

...a stricter penance was imposed than on the lesser sort of Christians.

Such, in brief, was the state of the people; but because it is not possible for any body or company of people to be properly governed unless certain particular persons have the oversight, management, and government of the affairs of the whole society, it follows that we must next investigate what sort of persons there were in the early Church who were specifically set apart to manage its affairs and to carry out its public services or ministries.

That God has always had a peculiar people, chosen for himself from among others, is too evident to need proof: such were the **Patriarchs** of old, the holy seed; such were the **Jews**, chosen by him above all other nations of the world. These were his <term>κλῆρος</term> <note>original Greek: "kleros," meaning a lot, portion, or inheritance</note>, his special lot and the portion of his inheritance; and this referred to the entire body of that people in general. 

But later, this title was confined within narrower limits and applied to that tribe which God had chosen to stand before him, to wait upon his altar, and to serve him in the exercise of religion. After the end of that dispensation <note>a "dispensation" refers to a specific period of divine history, in this case, the transition from the Old Testament law to the New Testament</note>, it was subsequently used in the ministry of the **Gospel** to signify those who, for the observance of the service of God, are specifically sanctified and set apart in the **Christian Church**: the **Clergy**, being those <note>original Latin: "qui divino cultui ministeria religionis impendunt"</note> "who devote the ministries of religion to divine worship," (ha-... <meta>The sentence continues on the next page; the prefix "ge-" indicates the start of a word like "geheiligd" (sanctified) or "geordineerd" (ordained).</meta>

This custom (although it may have been different in the Eastern Church) we are assured was always maintained in the Churches of Africa, until the time of Valerius, the predecessor of Augustine in his seat at Hippo (f). Valerius, being a Greek and possessing little skill in the Latin tongue, was unable to preach for the edification of the people; he therefore allowed Augustine, whom he had recently ordained as an Elder, to preach in his stead. This practice, although at first viewed unfavorably by some Bishops in those quarters, nevertheless soon became an example which other Churches followed.

Ischyras <note>A figure in a 4th-century ecclesiastical dispute who claimed to be a priest but had been ordained by a person of insufficient rank.</note>, because he was ordained by Colythus—who was no higher in rank than an **Elder** <note>Also known as a Presbyter; the author is arguing that an Elder does not have the authority to ordain others to the priesthood.</note>—(t) consequently had his ordination judged by the Council as null and of no value.

The local people were always present at every ordination or confirmation—especially those of the higher ministries—and they confirmed the action with their agreement and consent. Indeed, it cannot be denied that the people (particularly in some places) were held in high regard in this matter, so that such a thing seldom or never occurred without their presence and consent (u). To this end, before the **Bishop** ordained anyone, he was accustomed to present and make known to the people the names of those to whom the holy orders were to be given. This was done so that the people, as those who best knew the candidates' lives and conduct, might voice an objection if they had anything substantial to bring against them. (x) By this means, the unworthy were discovered and rejected, while those who were worthy were honored and admitted; thus the confirmation was made lawful and to the satisfaction of the people, having received—as **Cyprian** says—the common voice and consent without any objection being raised. For this reason, the **Clergy** (or the ecclesiastical persons), of whatever rank they might be, were said to be *proclaimed* <note>original: "prædicari"; to be publicly announced or nominated for office.</note>, made known, and presented. It furthermore clearly appears / that they had their set hours for prayer / namely the third, sixth, and ninth hour: This they had borrowed from the Jews, who divided the day into four great hours / the first, the third, the sixth, and the ninth hour, of which the three last were the appointed hours of prayer; The first hour began in the morning at six o'clock / and lasted until nine o'clock: The third from nine to twelve; and it was in these hours / that the Apostles and Christians were gathered / when the Holy Spirit descended upon them (d) <margin>(d) Acts 2:9, 15.</margin>; The sixth hour was from twelve to three o'clock in the afternoon; and it was at that time / that Peter climbed upon the roof to pray (e) <margin>(e) Acts 10:9.</margin>: The ninth was from three to six o'clock in the evening / and it was at that time / that Peter and John went up to the Temple / around the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour (f) <margin>(f) Acts 3:1.</margin>: This division was now maintained by the Christians in the following times / but whether they were maintained so precisely in their house-devotions / I cannot say for certain.

### Of the First Christians. Book 1. Chapter 9. ###

...the [Church] Fathers where the word *missa* <note>Latin for "dismissal." The Catechumens <note>New converts receiving instruction before baptism.</note> having departed, and the doors of the church being closed, they proceeded to the administration of the Lord's Supper, where only the believers were permitted to be present. There they prayed for all states and orders of men, gave the kiss of love <note>Also known as the "kiss of peace," a ritual greeting of fellowship.</note>, prayed for the *consecration* <note>The act of setting apart or hallowing the bread and wine.</note> or hallowing of the *Eucharist* <note>From the Greek *eucharistia*, meaning "thanksgiving."</note>, received the outward elements of the *Sacrament*, made their offerings, and the like; of which I shall not speak particularly at present, as I have intended to treat the *Sacrament* even more thoroughly hereafter; for which reason I also say nothing of their exhortations, church censures, *absolutions* <note>The formal pronouncement of forgiveness or the lifting of church discipline.</note>, etc., as these will be considered elsewhere—all the more because these things, though performed in the public assemblies, were nonetheless incidental and not ordinary parts of the divine service.

This is briefly the manner in which public worship was generally performed in those ancient times; which, although something was changed according to the circumstances of times or places, was nevertheless maintained in all respects as far as the principal part and the essence of the matter are concerned.

# of the First Christians. Book I, Chapter 9.

...the Fathers <note>The early Church Fathers, influential theologians of the first centuries of Christianity.</note> where the word *missa* <note>original: *missa* — Latin for "dismissal."</note> can be found, and they apply the same to their Mass; although they would have great difficulty bringing to light even one single passage from any good and approved Ecclesiastical Writer—at least from the first four hundred years—where that word was used in that sense as it is now understood. After the *Catechumens* <note>New converts receiving instruction before baptism.</note> had gone out and the doors of the Church were closed, they proceeded to the administration of the Lord’s Supper, at which only the faithful <note>Baptized members in full communion with the church.</note> were permitted to be present; there they then prayed for all states and orders of men, gave the kiss of love <note>The "kiss of peace," a traditional ritual greeting signifying Christian unity.</note>, prayed for the *Consecration* <note>original: *Consecratie* — the ritual sanctification of the bread and wine.</note> or hallowing of the *Eucharist* <note>original: *Eucharistie* — another name for the Lord's Supper or Holy Communion.</note>, received the outward elements of the *Sacrament*, made their offerings, and the like; of which I will not speak particularly at present, as I intend to deal more precisely with the *Sacrament* later; for which reason I also say nothing of their exhortations, church *censures* <note>original: *cenſuren* — formal discipline or reprimands for misconduct.</note>, *absolutions* <note>original: *abſolutien* — the formal pronouncement of forgiveness of sins.</note> etc., as these will be considered elsewhere, all the more because these things, although performed in the public Assemblies, were nonetheless only incidental, and not ordinary parts of the service of God.

This is briefly the manner in which, in those ancient times, public worship was generally performed, which—although some things were changed according to the circumstances of times or places—was nonetheless maintained in every way as far as the principal part and the essence of the matter are concerned.

# Of the Administration of Baptism

manner, how this **Sacrament** was administered in the ancient **Church**.

<margin>
(a) Tertullian, On Baptism, ch. 17, p. 230.
(b) Ibid. Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, p. 6.

Concerning the persons by whom this **Sacrament** was administered: these were the **Ministers** of the **Gospel**, the dispensers of the mysteries of **Christ** <note>In the early church, "mysteries" was the common term for the Sacraments.</note>, who then baptized and preached the **Gospel**, having been joined together in the same **Commission** by our **Savior**. It was commonly administered by the **Bishop**, called the <gloss>presiding one <note>original Greek: "πρόεδρως" (proedros)</note></gloss> by **Justin Martyr**, the <gloss>overseer <note>original Latin: "Antistes"</note></gloss> by **Tertullian**, and the **President** or principal **Minister** of the assembly—the <gloss>Highest Priest, who is the Bishop <note>original Latin: "Summus Sacerdos, qui est Episcopus"</note></gloss>, as he calls him (a); without whose permission and authority neither **Elders** <note>The Dutch "Ouderlingen" here refers to Presbyters or Priests.</note> nor **Deacons** might undertake to baptize, as not only **Ignatius** but also **Tertullian** expressly state (b). And when they did so, it was solely in cases of necessity, as is noted by an ancient writer (c) who lived in or around the time of **Cyprian**. The same is assured to us by **St. Jerome** as having been the custom in his time, although we find elsewhere that the ritual was begun by the **Bishop** but continued and completed by the **Elders** (d).

But as **Christianity** grew, this became an ordinary part of the office of the **Elders** and **Deacons**, and without doubt, it was administered by them more or less from the beginning; although they did not do so without his [the Bishop's] permission, out of reverence for the **Bishop** and to preserve the honor of the **church**, as **Tertullian** gives as the reason.

<margin>(i) *The Chaplet* <note>original: "De Coron. milit." (De Corona Militis)</note>, chapter 3, page 102.</margin>

It was also frequently taken in the morning before dawn, when they held their religious gatherings; *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman governor who wrote to Emperor Trajan about Christian practices around 112 AD</note> mentions this in his letter to the *Emperor* (k): 
<margin>(k) Book 10, Epistle 97.</margin>
for in times of persecution, when they were driven away by the searching malice of their enemies, they made use of the most secret corners and the most inconvenient hours, whenever they could come together to perform their religious duties. But this communicating in the evening or at night lasted only during the times of the fiercest persecutions, or was at least gradually abandoned: for *Cyprian* <note>Bishop of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD) and an influential Latin writer</note> (l) 
<margin>(l) *To Caecilius*, Epistle 63, page 104.</margin>
expressly argues against it, saying that it ought to occur in the morning. This practice then took the upper hand within a short time in almost all places in the world, except for some locations in *Egypt* around *Alexandria*, of which *Socrates* <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century historian of the Christian Church</note> (m) 
<margin>(m) As above, Page 287.</margin>
relates that after having feasted in the evening, they were accustomed to receive the *Sacrament*.

### On the Administration of the Lord’s Supper

...cause of its observation and correspondence with the Jewish Passover <note>The Jewish festival commemorating the Exodus; the author links the timing and nature of the first Eucharist to this feast</note>, and because at that time circumstances allowed no other way. It was administered by the Apostles, and the Christians alongside them, in the houses of the believers—and quite commonly in an upper room, which, through the generosity of certain Christians, was set apart for the service of the Congregation. As I have proven before, for the Christians living nearby, this was the fixed place set apart for their worship. Under the cruelties of the severe persecutions, they were forced to flee to the mountains, or to their *Cryptae* <note>original Latin: "Cryptae"; hidden underground chambers or vaults</note>, Caves, or subterranean passages, and to administer the Sacrament by the burial places of the Martyrs and over the ashes of the dead. 

But when the Churches began to become ornate and regular, they also began to administer various parts of the worship service each in a particular place within the church. The place for Communion was ordained at the upper or East end of the church, where it was administered upon a wooden table, which was later changed into one of stone. Both of these were almost universally called "Altars" by the Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers," influential early Christian theologians</note>—though improperly and by way of an allusion <note>original: "sin-speeling"; a metaphorical or symbolic reference rather than a literal sacrifice</note>—and even the Lord’s Supper itself, especially in later times, was called the "Sacrament of the altar." This place was called the *sanctuary* <note>original Greek: θυσιαστήριον (thusiastērion), literally "place of sacrifice" or "altar area"</note>, and it was separated by railings, within which the Clergy received the Sacrament, just as the common people did outside of them. It was here that they were all accustomed to come together for this Heavenly banquet; for

This is, for the most part, the order in which the first **Christians** administered this **Holy Sacrament**: For although I do not claim to have set everything down in that exact and precise order as it was always done (and how could I do such a thing, since it often changed according to the circumstances of time and place), nevertheless I do not doubt but that anyone who investigates the usage of those times will find that it happened as nearly as the nature of things could allow.

## Chapter II.

### *Concerning their Heavenly-mindedness, and contempt for the world.*

### C O N T E N T S.

The soul, when properly disposed, naturally reaches upward, especially when supported by the aid of Religion. The early Christians lived far above the world. No allurements of promises had any power over them. They considered it the greatest honor to be Christians. They were satisfied with a very meager portion of external things. The History of some of our Savior's Kindred, who were brought before *Domitian* <note>Titus Flavius Domitianus, Roman Emperor from 81 to 96 AD; he was known for his suspicion of potential rivals, including the relatives of Jesus.</note>. Their refusal to attend the Festivals and the games established for the people's amusement. Because of this, they were accused by the pagans. The soul of man, being of heavenly birth, cannot but participate in the nature and disposition of that Region, and have a natural inclination toward that place from which it has its origin: And although it is true that the same, in this corrupt and degenerate state, has sunk deep into the dust, and is burdened with the earthly and external affections of lower desires, and is as if shackled to them, with the desires and intentions of men creeping up and down like shadows over the surface of the earth; yet the same often aspires, especially when it is supported by the help of religion, toward its own release and freedom. ## Of Heavenly-Mindedness

> ...[to depart] from the world and hasten to seal our confession with our blood; as being certainly convinced that those who strive through their actions to prove themselves to be such as follow God, and heartily long for fellowship with Him in that life in which no wickedness or godlessness shall have place, will reach that state.

This was the strong staff upon which they leaned, the great strengthening of heart with which they sustained their spirits in those sorrowful times of suffering and persecution: the firm faith and the certain expectation they had of enjoying God in a better life. They knew that the more their enemies hastened to break open and set free the cage <note>The author uses the metaphor of a cage to describe the physical body holding the soul.</note> of their bodies, the sooner their souls would have the freedom to fly over to the lands of blessedness and immortality. And indeed, their thoughts were so set upon this, and they were accustomed to comforting one another so often by speaking of that Kingdom which they expected hereafter, that some of their enemies, hearing and misunderstanding these reasons, accused them of being traitors who were looking to seize the rule of the empire:

> ...those who would feign or deny such things, to avoid death and await a more convenient time to carry out our purposes; but since our hope is not fixed on anything in this world, we do not fear those who take our lives, well knowing that they take nothing from us but that which we must necessarily lay down ourselves.

In those times, it was their constant care to keep the thought of death vividly before them and to walk in the sight of eternity. This was generally true of all, just as Saint Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was a priest and scholar best known for translating the Bible into Latin, a version known as the Vulgate.</note> specifically relates of Marcella (b),

But beyond the influence and effect that the expectation of their own individual passing had upon them, there was something else which I do not doubt had great power to wean them from the world and strongly urge them toward a ready and swift diligence regarding the matters of the future life; and that was the feeling they commonly held, that the Day of Judgment was near. This was a sentiment that arose very early, as may be seen from the warning that Saint Paul gave to the Thessalonians regarding it (c),

> The Christians, he says, "dwell in their own land, but as guests and strangers; they share all things with other people as fellow citizens, and yet they endure all things as if they were foreign and alien; every foreign land is their Fatherland, and every Fatherland is foreign to them. They marry and father children just like other people, but they do not neglect or abandon their offspring as foundlings <note>This refers to the common Roman practice of "exposure," where unwanted infants were left outside to die or be taken by others.</note>. They share common meals, but do not indulge in excess <term>overdaat</term> <note>Meaning gluttony or unrestrained luxury.</note> as other people do. They are in the flesh, but they do not live according to the flesh. They walk upon the earth, but their conduct <term>wandel</term> <note>A term referring to one's entire manner of life and moral behavior.</note> is in Heaven." Therefore, he compares the Christians in this world to the soul in the human body; among other reasons, specifically this: that just as the soul lives in the body but is not *of* the body, so the Christians live in this world but are not *of* the world; just as an immortal spirit lives in a mortal tabernacle <note>A "tabernacle" here refers to a temporary shelter or tent, symbolizing the human body.</note>, so the Christians have their dwelling in these perishable abodes, while they look toward and expect an imperishable state in Heaven.

# CHAPTER III.

## *Concerning their modesty in regard to their clothing.*

### C O N T E N T S.

The disposition of the mind reveals itself freely in outward clothing. The primary reasons for clothing: for modesty, necessity, and distinction. The first Christians conformed themselves to these principles. They were careful not to be singular <note>Meaning they did not wish to look eccentric or draw unnecessary attention to themselves.</note>, nor to exceed their means. They commonly adapted themselves to the sober and modest fashion and custom of the places where they lived. Whether they, upon becoming Christians, laid aside the Roman robe <term>toga</term> <note>The formal garment of a Roman citizen.</note> and took up the cloak, or *pallium*. The proverb: *From the toga to the cloak* <note>original: "A toga ad pallium"</note>. The occasion on which Tertullian wrote his excellent book on that subject. The cloak was primarily worn by those who entered a life of more than common strictness <term>precijsheyt</term> <note>This refers to a life of asceticism or intense religious discipline.</note>. Their great care to maintain a middle ground between costliness and slovenliness: This was counted as a part of that pomp and vanity which they had renounced at Baptism. The vanity of costly clothes and excessive neatness lamented by the Church Fathers in some of those times. Their particular rebuke of the art of beautifying oneself <note>A reference to the use of cosmetics and elaborate hairstyling.</note>: What some in those days brought forward in defense of it, presented and answered from the Fathers. Their wealth was no sufficient proof to be allowed to do such things: Better ways to spend their goods were pointed out.

# CHAPTER IV.

->Concerning their great moderation in their food.<-

## C O N T E N T S.

Sinful fastidiousness regarding food and drink is a great temptation. Strictly forbidden by the Christian Law. The ancient Christians maintained such a rule of life as served for health; they cared not for comfort and delicacies. The great inconveniences of immoderation in food or drink. Their principal concern was for spiritual nourishment, being content with bare necessities, whatever they might be; Shown in various examples. The over-scrupulous and irreligious abstinence from certain kinds of food condemned. The example of the Martyr *Alcibiades*, from *Eusebius* <note>An early Christian historian (c. 260 – 339 AD), often called the "Father of Church History."</note>. The Christians were wrongly accused by the heathens of immoderation and extravagance in their meals. *Thyestean feasts* <note>original: "Thyestæa cœna" - a reference to the Greek myth of Thyestes, who was served his own children at a banquet. Romans used this term to accuse Christians of ritual cannibalism.</note>, or the eating of children, was charged against them. This accusation, in both its parts, was denied and completely refuted by *Tertullian* and other Defenders <note>or Apologists</note> of the Christians.

Among the manifold temptations that assault human life from all sides, there is hardly one by which we are more easily overcome than that of a

No dangers had the power then to draw Christians away from the performance of their duties. <margin>(g) To Antonianus, Epistle 52, p. 68.</margin> Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage and an important early Christian writer.</note> (g) highly praises Cornelius for having taken upon himself the Bishopric of Rome in such a dangerous time; he praises his courage, the immovable steadfastness of his faith, and the fearless acceptance of that position, precisely when the tyrant Decius <note>The Emperor Decius (reigned 249–251 AD), who initiated the first empire-wide organized persecution of Christians.</note> threatened the ministers of Christianity with such sorrowful cruelties, and would sooner tolerate a rival in the governance of the empire than have a Bishop hold his seat within Rome.

How boldly, and without regard for rank, did they speak what was in their hearts, even in the presence of their bitterest enemies? When Maris, Bishop of Chalcedon—a man who was blind from old age—had the opportunity to speak with the Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD), who attempted to revive Roman paganism and was the last non-Christian emperor.</note>, he boldly accused him of his atheism <note>original: "atheistery"; in this era, the term was often used to describe the rejection of the Christian God in favor of pagan idols.</note> and apostasy from the Christian faith. And when Julian reproached him for his blindness, and told him that his Galilean God <note>A derogatory term Julian used for Jesus Christ.</note> would never be able to restore his sight, that good old man answered him immediately: <margin>(h) Socrates Scholasticus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 3, ch. 12, p. 183.</margin> ,, "I thank my God that He has taken my sight from me, so that I should not see the face of him who has fallen into such great godlessness" (h).

unfold <note>likely the conclusion of "ontwikkelen," meaning to reveal or unfold</note> could be unknown to no one who merely considered the nature of their doctrine and the aim of their intent. The severity of their commandments, running so directly contrary to the corrupt and sinful inclinations of men; the purity of their religion, so clearly in conflict with the loose, unchaste, and foul church customs and ceremonies of the Pagans <note>original: *Heydenen*; referring to the non-Christian inhabitants of the Roman Empire</note>; their complete impossibility of being able to coexist with those religions which had already taken place for so many centuries, and had so firmly possessed and occupied the minds of men, and were secured and supported by all the powers and polities of the world, could portend no pleasant or welcome reception for them. 

This sect (for so they called it) was in every way not only contradicted, but also opposed: for since men have a natural reverence for antiquity, especially in matters of religion, they judge themselves obligated to stand up for a religion that has been handed down to them by their ancestors, and to set themselves with all power and might against all that might oppose it. 

The Great Ones of those times, and especially the Roman Emperors, made it their chief work to suppress, stifle, and banish this newborn religion from the world. From this arose those Imperial *Ordinances* <note>original: *Ordonantien*; official decrees or laws</note>, which were sent daily to all parts of the Roman Empire, to give their *Governors* <note>original: *Gouverneurs*; provincial rulers like Pontius Pilate or Pliny the Younger</note> command and power toward the ruining and destroying

# Concerning Endurance

...is to be noted—namely—the magnitude of those pains and that suffering which Christians in general had to undergo, and then how they conducted themselves therein.

The first, regarding the great pains and sorrows they endured, they were as cruel as the intellect and the malice of men or devils could devise. In this regard, we shall first take a view of the more common or ordinary punishments commonly used by the Greeks and Romans, and thereafter, those which were used against the Christians beyond ordinary custom <note>The author distinguishes between legal Roman capital punishments and the "extraordinary" tortures specifically invented or escalated during persecutions.</note>.

Among their ordinary modes of punishment, these six stood out primarily: the cross, the rack <term>pijn-bank: a frame for stretching the body to displace joints</term>, the wheel, burning, wild beasts, and condemnation to the mines <note>original: "berg-werken"; this referred to "Damnatio ad metalla," a sentence of forced labor in mines or quarries, which was effectively a slow death sentence due to the brutal conditions.</note>.

I. The cross deserves the first place in our enumeration, not only because it was one of the oldest and most common modes of punishment among the heathens and introduced by them among the Jews, but also because it was the instrument by which our blessed Savior <note>The "Zaligmaker" refers to Jesus Christ.</note> himself was put to death. Now, without speaking of its various and different forms and types, all of which were used against the early Christians, I look here only at that which was the most common: there was a straight piece of wood that stood in the ground; at the upper end, or nearly at the top of it, a cross-beam was attached, so that it was not unlike the letter T.

<meta>This page continues the description of the cross as a Roman instrument of execution, specifically detailing the physical structure and the dual nature of the punishment: its intense physical pain and the profound social shame it carried.</meta>

### Of the First Christians. Book II, Chapter 7.

...was—although it is probable that another piece of wood still protruded above the crossbeam. In this kind of punishment, there were two things that made it cruel: namely, the pain and the shame. It was necessarily painful because the sufferer, having nails driven through the hands and feet, was fastened to it; since these are the parts where the nerves converge, it inevitably caused sharp and sensitive wounds. Furthermore, because these parts are far from the vital or primary organs of the body, death became tedious and slow, making the pain two or even threefold more severe. Indeed, some—out of a generous compassion—had the criminals strangled first before they were crucified, as Julius Caesar did regarding the pirates to whom he had sworn the death of the cross <note>original: "kruys dood"</note> (h):

<margin>(h) Suetonius, *Life of Julius Caesar*, chapter 74, page 76.</margin>

But this favor was not granted to the Christians; for they were left to hang in the midst of all those agonizing death-pains until they died of hunger, or the "mercy" of wild beasts or birds of prey brought them death (i).

<margin>(i) Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 8, chapter 8, page 300.</margin>
<margin>(k) Roman Martyrology, for the day of November 30, page 736.</margin>

Thus St. Andrew <note>The apostle Andrew is traditionally said to have been crucified on an X-shaped cross, though this text focuses on his endurance.</note> remained alive on the cross for two whole days, teaching the people all that time (k); and Timothy, with his wife Maura, having been hung on the cross after many other tortures, hung there for nine days before they completed their martyrdom (l).

<margin>(l) The same [Roman Martyrology], for the day of May 3, page 272.</margin>

II. The rack, called in Latin the *equuleus* <note>A torture device named after a "little horse," because the victim's position resembled a rider.</note>, was so named either because of the posture of the criminal's body on that bench—resembling a person sitting on a horse—or because of the hoisting of a person by cords and pulleys. Its primary purpose was to torture the guilty or suspected persons to force them to confess the truth (p). Scholars do not all agree on exactly what its physical form was, but we may, in all likelihood, understand it thus: there was an instrument made of several pieces of timber, all fastened together, on the upper side of which the suffering person was laid on his back on a long plank, and thus fastened by the hands and feet.
