...were, with the assurance that if they would only deny Christ, he would promote them to wealth and status; so—
<margin>(x) The same, p. 81. <note>original: "Ibid. p. 81." Referring to the same source mentioned on the previous page, likely the sermons of Saint Basil the Great.</note></margin>
—was their answer (x), that he placed his snares in the wrong place; that he could not give them what he sought to take from them; that they could not accept his offers, unless they wished to suffer infinite loss through this negotiation; that it was of no use to offer a small advantage of the world to those who despised the whole world; that all visible advantages were nothing in comparison to what they held in hope and expectation, since all the beauty and glory of Heaven and earth cannot be compared to that state of blessedness <note>A term often used in older theology to describe the supreme happiness of heaven.</note> which is the portion of the righteous; the one being of short duration and passing, and the other constant and everlasting: that they were not desirous of any gift, except only the crown of righteousness <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 4:8, symbolizing the reward for a faithful life.</note>, nor sought any other honor than the heavenly one: that they feared no pain except that of hell, and of that fire which is truly terrible: And as for the punishments now inflicted upon them, they considered them merely as the strokes of a child, and the ill-treatment of their bodies—however long it lasted—as a ready path to a more beautiful crown. Such was the mind of those Christian soldiers <term>Christian-krijgsknechten: literally "Christian war-servants." The Forty Martyrs were elite Roman soldiers of the Legio XII Fulminata.</term>, those upright champions for the Christian faith; and so they strengthened and comforted one another.

# On Justice #

...barbaric and inhumane practice of the **Gnostics** <note>A diverse group of early religious movements that claimed secret knowledge (gnosis) and were often criticized by early Church Fathers for their unconventional or supposedly immoral rituals.</note> mentioned by *Irenaeus* and *Epiphanius*.

Having briefly spoken of the Religion of the early Christians, as it regarded their piety toward God, and their moderation and virtuous conduct regarding themselves, we shall now, in the final place, consider them with regard to their behavior toward others. This behavior is described by the Apostle <note>A common reference to St. Paul.</note> under the name of **justice** <note>original: *rechtveerdigheyt*. This term translates to both "justice" and "righteousness," referring here to the social and legal integrity one owes to their neighbor.</note>. Under this term, he includes all those duties and regards which we must and do exercise toward others, of which we shall note and present the following proofs: Their justice and integrity in matters of trade and commerce; their love and mutual affection for one another; their concord and peaceableness; and their obedience and submission under the civil government.

I begin with the first: their just and upright conduct in their outward dealings. It is one of the great objectives of Christ’s Law to confirm and approve that great fundamental rule, which is one of the first and fundamental laws of nature: **to harm no one, and to give each his due** <note>original: *niemand te beledigen, en elk een het zijne te geven*. This is a translation of the famous Roman legal principle: *alterum non laedere, suum cuique tribuere*.</note>. This is to teach us that we must behave as befits our relationship with other men. Beside the exercise of duty which we owe to God, the **Gospel** <note>original: *Euangelium*</note> obliges us to be just, upright, and sincere in all our dealings toward men, not

> "If a Christian falsely accused another before the Church (for in those times it was permitted to appeal to the pagan judgment seats <note>The secular Roman courts.</note>) then he was punished,"

(that is, kept away from the **Lord's Supper**, which was the only punishment the Church at that time could impose on anyone) according to the nature of the crime which he had charged against the other, according to the 

<margin>(q) Council of Elvira, Canon 74, Page 79, where see the notes of Albaspinaeus <note>original: "Albaſp." Gabriel de l'Aubespine (1579–1630), a French bishop and scholar of early church law.</note></margin>

> "decision of the **Council of Elvira** (q), which decreed that when someone proved his accusation, yet had kept it hidden for a significant time without revealing it, he should be kept away from the **Lord’s Supper** for two years."

The probable reason for this was that, by keeping the matter secret, the guilty party had been given the opportunity to infect others, allowing their sinful example to spread to the rest of the community. But so that no door would be opened to such accusations, and the malicious would not be encouraged in them, it was ordered

## Of Justice

> ...even if they <note>Referring to the pagan accusers.</note> themselves could not be guilty of such things, they should not think such of the **Christians**, who, like other people, were instructed with the same fundamental laws of humanity; that they were so far from favoring murder or manslaughter

> (h) that, on the contrary, it was judged unlawful among them to be present at the **gladiatorial combats** <note>original: "kamp-vechten"; combat games in the arena where fighters often died for entertainment.</note>, in which human life was so recklessly sacrificed to the pleasure and curiosity of the people; 

<margin>(i) Athenagoras, as above. Minucius Felix, as above. Tertullian, as above, chapter 9.</margin>

> that (i) they considered it a homicide if a woman, through evil arts, caused an **abortion** <note>original: "mis-geboorte"; here referring to a medically or magically induced termination of pregnancy.</note> to smother the fruit, or to kill a child in any way before it receives its life; since it is surely the same thing to prevent life or to take life—to kill a human or to destroy that which would become a human—given that he who kills the fruit in its seed truly destroys it. That it was not probable that **Christians** would find pleasure in eating human blood, as they ate no blood at all, abstaining even from **strangled blood** <note>original: "gestikte bloed"; referring to the Apostolic Decree in Acts 15:29, which prohibited eating blood or the meat of animals that had not been bled properly.</note>. And that the **heathens** <note>original: "heydenen"</note> themselves had to admit this when they, among many tricks used to discover if someone was a **Christian**, offered them bladders full of blood—knowing well that it was unlawful for them to taste any blood; and that it was therefore entirely improbable that they, who had an aversion even to the blood of animals, would thirst for human blood.

# Of Righteousness

...had been devised by malicious heretics: But there is little reason to doubt the truth of that matter, as **Epiphanius** assures us (r),
<margin>(r) In the same place <note>original: "Ibid."</note>, p. 48.</margin>
that he received what he relates from the mouths of the **Gnostics** themselves; and that not only had many women, who were led astray into these abominable errors, revealed this to him, but that he himself in his younger years, when he was in **Egypt**, was solicited by them, and was tempted to join them through all the arts of flattery and persuasion, of wantonness and unchastity. And certainly, it is unthinkable that someone who was so venerable on account of his learning and godliness as **Epiphanius** would have wished to deceive us by the fabrication of such great and manifest falsehoods. Moreover, anyone who simply reads **Irenaeus**—in whose time that heresy was most prevalent and had the upper hand—and considers what he relates about it, and what he had heard from those who had returned from their ranks to the Church, will see little reason to think that any godlessness is too great to charge them with, or to doubt the truth of what he relates concerning them.

That the Christian religion intends, above all else, the implementation and perfection of the fundamental principles of human nature is evident—among many other proofs—particularly from this: that it so strictly commands, cultivates, and promotes natural courtesy and compassion, which are among the first and most essential inclinations of mankind. Wherever the Gospel is accepted from the heart, it gives rise to such a sweet and pleasant disposition of the mind that it makes us humble, communicative, courteous, and benevolent—inclined and fit for every good work, and worthy in all the duties of courtesy and friendliness. ### Of the First Christians. Book III, Chapter 2.

„ ...abundantly blessed, having allowed me to see that you have forsaken the happiness of this life and have passed over into His household and service: And therefore, what do I do here any longer?“

Indeed, they had such great zeal in those times for the souls of men, that many did not even shrink from entering into physical slavery for no other purpose than to deliver others from their spiritual slavery. Thus it was that **Serapion** (called **Sindonites** because he never wore more than a single poor linen garment <note>original: "Sindonites," derived from the Greek *sindon*, a fine linen cloth or shroud</note>), one of the first **Ascetics** <term>Ascetics: individuals who practiced rigorous self-denial and lived a simple life for religious devotion</term> (u), sold himself

<margin>(u) Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 83, in the *Life of Serapion*, page 182.</margin>

to a pagan stage-actor, with whom he lived and performed the most menial services, until he had converted him, his wife, and his entire family to Christianity. When they were baptized, they restored him to his freedom; he, in turn, gave back the money he had received as the price of his servitude, which by mutual consent was given to the poor. Coming later to **Lacedemon** <note>The ancient name for the city-state of Sparta</note>, and hearing that a prominent person of the City—otherwise a very good man—was infected with the **Manichaean heresy** <note>A dualistic belief system that was a major rival to early Christianity; it taught that the world was a struggle between good/light and evil/darkness</note>, it was one of the first things he did to introduce himself to that household and sell himself as a slave. In this situation, he remained for two whole years, until he had brought his master and his entire household away from that harmful heresy and back to the Church; who not only thanked God for it, but also him

### Of Love and Beneficence

"...not acting as a servant, but with such affection and respect as one owes to a brother and a father."

Such was the good nature and spirit of the Christians in those times! They sought and aimed entirely at the happiness of mankind and were inclined and eager to liberally share the treasures of the Gospel, wishing even that all people were as rich and happy in that regard as they were themselves. They were far from that malicious accusation that **Celsus** <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and one of the first major intellectual critics of Christianity</note> brought against them—as if they, should all people want to become Christians, would not allow it;

<margin>(x) Against Celsus, Book 3, p. 116.</margin>
for **Origen** <note>A prominent early Christian scholar and theologian who wrote a famous defense against Celsus</note> (x) flatly contradicts that lie and tells him that its falsehood could be proven by the fact that the Christians, as much as was in them, were not reluctant to spread their doctrine throughout the entire world; and that some of them had particularly undertaken to travel back and forth, not only in the cities but in hamlets and villages, to win others over to the true religion. And that they, he says, did not do this out of any aim for profit or advantage is clear, because they often did not even accept necessary provisions from others; and if they did so, it was only such as was entirely and absolutely necessary for them at that time, even though great acts of charity were often offered to them. Indeed, even

<margin>(y) Council of Carthage 3, Canon 18.</margin>
some ancient **Canons** <term>Canons: laws or decrees made by a church council to regulate doctrine or discipline</term> (y) expressly require that no one who [held] either heretical or

# Of Love and Charity

...the sick, which afflicted not only the heathens, but however also the Christians. Many of the brethren, says the historian <margin>(o) Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 7, chapter 22, page 269. <note>Eusebius of Caesarea was a 4th-century scholar and the first great historian of the Christian Church.</note></margin> (o), out of an uncommon greatness and abundance of their affection and love, without in any way considering their own lives or safety, cast themselves into the greatest dangers. They daily visited and tended to the sick and infected brothers, instructing and comforting them until they gave up their spirit and died with them. Indeed, many of those whom they served in this way were restored and remained alive, while those who had served them died themselves, as if, through a strange and wondrous benevolence, they were willing to take the others' illnesses upon themselves and die so that the others might be kept from death. Such was the condition of the Christians, while at the same time the heathens rejected all sense of humanity and affection. For whenever someone among them began to fall sick, they threw that person out of the house, shunned their dearest friends and kinsmen, abandoned them on the public roads, and took no care for them, whether they were alive or dead.

But so that this work of charity might be better maintained among the Christians, they had in many places (and particularly in Alexandria) certain persons whose specific office was to tend to the sick and serve them. These were called *Parabolani*, for the reason that they—especially during pestilential and infectious diseases—were accustomed to risk their lives <note>original Greek: <term>παραβάλλεσθαι</term> (*paraballesthai*), meaning to expose oneself to danger or to venture one’s life.</note>, which is/

<summary>This page contrasts the self-sacrificial care Christians showed during plagues—often dying so that others might live—with the abandonment practiced by their pagan neighbors. It introduces the Parabolani, a group of early Christian healthcare workers in Alexandria who specialized in nursing the infectious.</summary>

### of the First Christians. Book III. Ch. 2.
<meta>catchword: lijke</meta>

<margin>(p) Theodosian Code, book 16, Title 2, regarding Bishops, and 42, 43. <note>The Theodosian Code was a 5th-century compilation of Roman laws under the Christian emperors.</note></margin>
...is to cast themselves into certain dangers of their lives; and they were specifically ordained <term>to care for the sick bodies of the weak <note>original: "ad curanda debilium aegra corpora"</note></term>, as the law of the younger *Theodosius* expresses it (p), that is, to look after the diseased bodies of the infirm. The number of these same individuals seems to have been quite large, because, in the event of any riot, even the courts of civil justice had a dread of them; wherefore the Emperor *Theodosius*, upon the complaint made to him regarding this, reduced their number to five hundred. However, this number being found too small, he expanded their number to six hundred through a second Ordinance. Be that as it may, it is certain that these *Parabolani* <term>Parabolani: A group of early Christian medics who risked their lives—the name comes from the Greek word for "risk-takers"—to care for the sick and bury the dead during plagues.</term> were a kind of Ecclesiastical Physicians: for it is clear that they had an ecclesiastical character or were under church authority, because they were counted among the *Clergy* or church officials, and by the last Ordinance of *Theodosius* it was ordered that they should be chosen by the Bishop of that place and be immediately subject to him.

<margin>(q) Ambrose, *On Duties*, book 2, chapter 15, page 42.</margin>

A fourth evidence of that first love and charity was their great care for the bodies of the dead, giving them a fitting <margin>(d)</margin> and, where they were able, an honorable burial. All people have a natural affection for their bodies and wish, therefore, that that which has so long been the dwelling-place of an immortal inhabitant <note>This refers to the soul inhabiting the body.</note> be laid down in an orderly fashion upon its departure, and that its remains be gathered with honor and in safety. The human body—besides being a cabinet <margin>(a)</margin> in which an invaluable jewel <note>The soul.</note> is enclosed—is a neat and elegant work of art, wonderfully made in an awesome manner <note>original: "op een vreesslijke wijse wonderbaarlijk gemaakt," an allusion to the Biblical phrase "fearfully and wonderfully made" from Psalm 139:14.</note>, and an excellent composition of divine omniscience and omnipotence; it therefore deserves not to be carelessly thrown away or unsuitably trodden into the mire. 

This appears to be the common feeling of all people, and the care and practice of nearly all nations in the world: to piously place the remains of one's deceased friends in tombs and sepulchers, judging it to be no more than reasonable to show such affection for dead friends, honoring their memory, and safely preserving that which they leave behind—having cast off mortality—from wild and barbaric violence and nuisance. This was, I know for certain, <margin>(b)</margin> in an outstanding manner the care of the Christians; no dangers or threats could deter them from this final duty to their deceased brothers, especially those martyrs...

They also ensured not only that the body was well prepared for burial, but also that it might be laid away honorably and safely in a suitable and proper grave; a practice that has always been observed by the most sober and well-mannered of people. This was because all nations have held the *disturbing of the buried shades* <note>original Latin: *Manes temerare sepultos*</note>—to disturb or desecrate the ashes of the dead—to be an act of great godlessness. Truly, the multitude of **Martyrs** who suffered then required a very large space for their proper burial; and they had this, so that the author who recently published *Roma Subterranea* <note>Referring to Antonio Bosio's 1632 work "Roma Subterranea," the first systematic study of the Roman catacombs.</note> assures us (a) <margin>(a) Book 1, ch. 2, no. 9, p. 4.</margin> that although these <term>cemeteries</term> <note>original: *Cæmeteria*</note> were under the earth, they were nonetheless often two or sometimes three stories high, with one burial place being made beneath the other.

Being underground, they were necessarily quite dark, having no light from the outside except what could enter through a few small cracks. This filled the place with a kind of holy dread, as **Jerome** relates (b) <margin>(b) <note>original: *Comm. in c. 40. Ezech. tom. 5. p. 521.*</note> **Jerome**, *Commentary on Ezekiel*, Chapter 40, Volume 5, p. 521.</margin>, who in his youth, while attending school in **Rome**, was accustomed to visit these solemn places on the Lord’s day.

They were built by pious and generous people, from whom they also took their names, for the burial of the **Martyrs**...

"In this sad and wretched case," cried Cyprian, then Bishop of that <margin>(d) Pontius, in *The Life of Cyprian*, p. 13.</margin> place, "(d) called the Christians together, instructed them in the duties of compassion and love, and made them remember that it was no great wonder if they extended their love and charity toward those who were of their own party <note>Meaning their fellow believers.</note>; that the way to be perfect was to do something more than the pagans <term>heydenen; non-Christians or polytheists</term> and tax collectors <note>A reference to the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:46-47).</note>, to overcome evil with good, to follow the divine mercy <term>goedertierentheyt; a term for God's loving-kindness</term>, to love our enemies, and, according to the counsel of our Lord, to pray for the well-being of those who persecute us; that God constantly makes His sun to rise and His rain to fall, not only for the benefit of His own children, but also for all other people; and that therefore they, who professed to be His children, should follow the example of such a Father. 

Upon this, they all immediately agreed with one mind to assist their common enemies, each one lending his help according to his rank and status; those who, because of their poverty, had nothing to give or to contribute, did that which was greater: laboring and working around the sick in their own person—a support that surpassed all other gifts...

## CHAPTER III.

### Concerning the unity and peacefulness of the first Christians.

-> C O N T E N T S <-

The laws of Christ aim to cultivate a peaceful disposition. This was evident in our Savior Himself, in His Apostles, and the entire body of Christians. What *Justin Martyr* relates concerning this. Before the coming of *Christ*, the world was overrun with discord. The happy change that followed His appearance. This is extensively shown by *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea was a 4th-century historian often called the "Father of Church History."</note>. How much the Christians contributed to the peace and tranquility of the world. Their unity among one another. The *Canonical Letters* <note>These were formal letters used by the early Church to verify the identity and standing of Christians traveling between different regions</note>. The various types of the same: Commendatory, Dismissory, and Peaceable letters <note>original: Συστατικαὶ, ἀπολυτικαὶ, εἰρηνικαὶ (Systatikai, apolytikai, eirēnikai). These Greek terms refer to the specific legal and ecclesiastical categories of letters that allowed Christians to find hospitality and fellowship in distant cities.</note>. Their nature and purpose. Their efforts to settle disputes immediately. The great care and concern of *Constantine* <note>The Roman Emperor Constantine the Great, who sought to end theological divisions to maintain imperial stability.</note> regarding this. An excellent example of *Gregory Nazianzen*, in his self-denial and yielding for the sake of the peace of the Church. Differences in Church customs and lesser matters were no hindrance to peace and Christian fellowship: Shown in the case of *Polycarp* and *Anicetus*, Bishop of *Rome* <note>Polycarp and Anicetus famously disagreed on the date of Easter in the 2nd century but maintained communion despite their differences.</note>. Christians were not incited against one another by all... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

<header>Of Subjection</header>

# CHAPTER IV.

## On their obedience and submission to civil government.

->SUMMARY.<-

Government is the great bond of public peace. This is most highly secured by Christianity. The laws of Christ regarding this are clear and positive. Confirmed by his own practice, and by that of the Apostles. The same was demonstrated in the following centuries, shown from *Justin Martyr* <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD) was an early Christian apologist who wrote to the Emperor to explain Christian beliefs.</note>, *Polycarp* <note>Polycarp (69–155 AD), the Bishop of Smyrna and a disciple of the Apostle John.</note>, and *Origen*. Prayers for Rulers and Emperors were a solemn part of their public worship. Their willing payment of tolls and taxes, and their sincerity therein. Christians remained so even under the most grievous oppressions and persecutions, and even then, when they had the power to justify and avenge themselves. A notable passage regarding this from *Tertullian* <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) was a prolific Christian author from Carthage who defended the faith against Roman accusations.</note>. The conduct of Christian soldiers in the army of *Julian* <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman emperor who attempted to suppress Christianity.</note>. # Of Submission

...how the first Christians, because of their submission and subjection under civil government, excelled above all others. Indeed, there is hardly anything in which the first Christians triumphed more before the world than in their exemplary obedience to the **Powers** and **Authorities** under whom they lived—honoring their persons, respecting their power, paying their taxes, and obeying their laws, whenever they were not clearly contrary to the laws of *Christ* <note>original Latin: "Christi"</note>. For if the laws did conflict with their faith, they submitted themselves, with the greatest stillness and tranquility of their souls, to the cruelest punishments inflicted upon them. It is certain that one of the primary objectives of the Christian law is to ensure and establish the interests of civil power. Our **Savior** explicitly taught us to give unto the Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s (a). And his Apostles speak as clearly as words allow: "Let every soul," says *Paul* (b), "be subject to the powers set over them. For there is no power but from God, and the powers that exist are ordained by God, so that whoever resists the power, resists the ordinance of God, and those who resist shall bring judgment upon themselves. Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only for the sake of punishment, but also for the sake of conscience. For this reason you also pay taxes <term>translated from the Dutch "schattinge," meaning tribute or tax payments to the state</term>, for they are God’s servants, continually attending to this very thing. # On Obedience

.. justice owed: from you we receive wages for our labor, but from Him we have received our very life and being. In this matter, we cannot obey the Emperor in such a way that we would deny God / the author of our existence / and indeed / whether you wish to acknowledge it or not / the author of your life as well. It is not out of despair, Sire / (which always speaks most boldly in the greatest of distresses) / that we speak so freely against you: we possess weapons (as you see) / yet we offer no resistance / choosing rather to die than to conquer / and desiring rather to die innocent / than to live as rebels or seekers of vengeance. If you have resolved to subject us to greater and more grievous pains / we are ready / to receive them. We are Christians / and therefore we cannot hide that we are such. You will necessarily have to acknowledge the invincible courage of this regiment; we lay down our arms; Your officials will find our right hands unarmed / but our breasts armed with a sincere Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or orthodox Christian faith of the early church, prior to the Great Schism or the Reformation.</note> faith. Kill us / trample upon us, we surrender our necks to the swords of the executioners with undaunted courage: These things are all the more welcome to us / because / being thus rejected by you / we shall pass with all haste to the heavenly crown.

-># On Submissiveness<-

We see the injustice of that accusation which the Pagans <note>original: "Heydenen"</note> sometimes laid upon the Christians: that they were disturbers of the common peace and enemies of civil government; a testimony so patently false, and without any shadow of a practical pretext to justify it, that even the ingenious Pagan in [the writings of] Minutius Felix <note>Marcus Minucius Felix was one of the earliest Latin Christian apologists; he wrote the dialogue *Octavius* to defend Christianity against pagan claims.</note>—though he brought forward all the slanders he could, and applied the greatest gloss and color that intellect and eloquence could provide to every accusation—nevertheless did not have the audacity to even mention such a thing once. Nevertheless, however groundless it was, the Christians were generally accused of this. Sometimes they were accused of faithlessness and treason, either because they would not swear by the spirit <note>original: "genius" — in Roman religion, the *genius* was the individual divine spirit of a person, and swearing by the Emperor's *genius* was a test of political loyalty.</note> of the emperor, or would not sacrifice for his safety, or because they would not honor and worship the emperors as divine beings <note>original: "Divos"</note> or gods, nor celebrate his feast days in the same manner as others. Regarding the first point—their refusal to swear by the spirit of the Emperor—we have previously heard what Tertullian <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note> answers to this: "that it was, in fact, the same as showing divine honor to devils." Regarding the second point—their not sacrificing for the emperor’s safety—the same Father 

<margin>(a) Apology, chapter 30, page 27 <note>original: "Apol. c. 30. p. 27."</note></margin>

answers (a): "that no one sacrificed to such a godly end as they did: for they offered their prayers to the true, living, and eternal God for the preservation of the emperor, so that God, whose..."

> » [after] having prayed for forgiveness, he was absolved and readmitted into the fellowship of the **Church**. Anyone who wishes to know more of this can find that **History** described at length by **Theodoretus**. (q)
<margin>(q) Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 15.</margin>

This severity was used against those who had transgressed, partly to make them more sensitive to their sins, partly to instill fear and dread in others, but primarily to give satisfaction to **God** and His **Kerke** regarding the truth and sincerity of their repentance. From this it follows that this penitence is so often called "satisfactions" in the writings of those times. For whenever the **Fathers** <note>The "Church Fathers" were influential Christian theologians and writers in the first few centuries after Christ.</note> use this word, it refers either to **men** or to **God**.

<margin>
<unclear>(a) Summa, Second part of the Second part, question 8, article 1.</unclear>
</margin>

**If** it refers to **men**, then the meaning is that through these outward acts of sorrow and mortification <note>In this context, "mortification" refers to physical acts of self-denial, such as fasting or wearing sackcloth, intended to humble the spirit.</note>, they satisfied the **Church** concerning their repentance and rectified the offense and scandal they had caused by their sins (r).

<margin>(r) Augustine, Enchiridion, chapter 65, volume 3.</margin>

**If** it refers to **God**, then it was taken as the acknowledgment of man's sin and the praying for remission and forgiveness. Thus it is that **Cyprianus**, speaking of the state of unrepentant sinners, magnifies their fault because they *sinned, but did not make satisfaction* <note>original: "peccabant, nec satisfaciebant"</note>; they sinned, but did not satisfy—that is (as he explains in the following words), they neither confessed nor wept for their sins. And speaking previously of **God**, [stating] that He is the only object of tears and sorrow over sin, to whom—and not to **men**—these [tears] must be sent, he says: »

God, who must be satisfied through satisfaction; who, being greatly angered, must be petitioned through a long-lasting and complete repentance, as He alone can forgive the sins committed against Him. So it was that the satisfaction, which they intended to give to God, consisted of seeking to turn away His displeasure and to regain His forfeited favor through a deep sorrow and <term>contrition</term> <note>A state of feeling remorseful and penitent for one's sins.</note> over sin, through a prompt acknowledgment and detestation of their crimes, and by humbly giving honor to God, both for His mercy and His justice.

<margin>(s) On Penitence <note>original Latin: "De pœnit."</note>, chapter 8, pages 126, 127.</margin>
For this reason, confession is called by **Tertullian** (s) the counsel, or the purpose, of satisfaction. And a little later he describes it thus: "Confession," he says, "is that through which we acknowledge our crime before **God**, not as if He did not know it, but insofar as through that confession the satisfaction is furthered, the repentance is produced, and through the repentance **God** is satisfied." In this sense it is often used by Him (by **Cyprian**) and by others, which I note all the more gladly in order to point out the absurd and ungodly doctrine so common among the <term>Papists</term> <note>A historically derogatory term used by Protestants to refer to Roman Catholics.</note>, which they even claim to have from these **Fathers** themselves: namely, that through the works of <term>penitence</term> <note>Acts of religious discipline or self-punishment to show sorrow for sin.</note> restitution is made to **God** for the obligation to the punishment that was created by the sin, whereby at least the temporal punishments that the sins have deserved are meritoriously taken away, and reconciliation is obtained. Having now seen the severity of the discipline or correction in the ancient Church, nothing remains but for us to marvel at and become followers of their godliness and sincerity, of their infinite hatred of sin, and of their care and zeal to preserve that strictness and purity of life which made their religion so famous in the world and caused it to triumph. If this discipline were restored to its proper strength, what a happy thing it would be for the Christian world! This is the judgment and the wish especially of our own (English) Church, which, regarding the solemn penance and humiliation of the **Lenten season**, states in the preface to the "Commination" <note>original: "bedreyging"—referring to the Commination service in the Book of Common Prayer, a service of "denouncing of God's anger and judgments against sinners" used on Ash Wednesday.</note>:

Acacius sells the silver of the Church to set captive enemies free. Page 542.
Acilius Glabrio, Consul <note>original: "Burgermeester." While literally "Mayor," in the context of ancient Rome, this refers to the office of Consul.</note> of Rome, killed by Domitian for the sake of the Christian religion. 38.
Acolyte <note>A minor clerical office in the early church, assisting the higher clergy.</note>, the nature of his office. 207.
*Agapai* <note>original Greek: Αγάπαι. Communal meals shared by early Christians, also known as "love-feasts."</note>. See *Love-feasts*.
Hadrian, a Pagan Emperor, commands that Christians should not be punished unless they are first convicted. 78.
Idolatry described: called a crime of the first rank, etc., by a Council in Spain, 86; who was judged guilty of it. *Ibid*. 619, 620; those guilty of the same, how they were ecclesiastically censured. 92, 93; refused by the first Christians along with the resignation of their offices, 94; opposed at the risk of their lives. 100; punished with withholding of the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Avondmaal," literally "Evening Meal."</note>, and sometimes even until death. 296; chosen in order to avoid committing fornication. 399; escaped by running into a burning furnace. 435; not with violence, but through friendly reasoning and prayers. 596.
Agatha gives reasons why she humbled herself to the service of the lowliest. 330.
Alexander Severus had great respect for Christ because of His excellent commandments, especially that one should do unto others what one wishes to be done unto oneself. 491.
Altar, or Communion Table <note>original: "Avondmaals-tafel."</note>, the same thing: why it was so named. 122, 125; in the first Churches it was a wooden table. 124; it was not fixed in place and was not adorned. 125; it was not an actual altar. 302; the lack of such altars was a reproach against them [the Christians] by pagans. 125; changed into fixed ones, of stone and marble, and when: in time they became places of reverence and *asyla* <note>Latin: sanctuaries or places of refuge.</note>, or places of safety. 126.
Ambrose did not fast on Saturdays in Milan, but [did]...
